    1. When doing the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, the sample with the least number of observations, X, has t observations. The sample with the largest number of observations, Y, has x observations. What is the maximum and minimum value of the test statistic, W?
    1. A data scientist at a regional bank wants to perform a Wilcoxon rank-sum test on financial data, but is unsure of the steps involved. For each of the steps in the Wilcoxon rank-sum test procedure below, assign the order in which the step comes in the testing procedure.
    • Get the critical value for the test based on the pre-selected type I error rate. For a left tailed test, the critical value will be \(n(n+m+1)-c\). For a right tailed test, the critical value will be \(c\). \(c\) is the critical value from Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
    • Create the null and alternative hypotheses regarding the difference betweeen the medians of the two independent populations. That is, \(H_0: \mu_1-\mu_2= \delta_0, H_a: \mu_1-\mu_2 (\neq, >, <) \delta_0\).
    • For the smaller sample \(X\), subtract \(\delta_0\) from each \(X\). The \(X\) sample becomes (\(X_i-\delta_0\)) for \(i=1, 2, ..., n\).
    • Order the combined sample from smallest to largest.
    • Reject the null hypothesis or fail to reject the null hypothesis depending on whether the test statistic, \(w\), is greater than the critical value.
    • Pool the \(n\) (\(X-\delta_0\)) observations and the \(m\) \(Y\) observations into one sample of size \(n+m\).
    • Calculate the test statistic, \(w\), by summing the ranks corresponding to the (\(X-\delta_0\)) observations in the pooled sample.
    • Label the smaller sample \(X\) and the larger sample \(Y\). That is, if one sample has \(m\) observations and another sample has \(n\) observations, and \(n<m\), label the sample with \(n\) observations as \(X\) and the sample with \(m\) observations as \(Y\).
    • Rank the observations in the combined sample from smallest to largest.
  1. An ecologist in Houston, Texas, is trying to analyze how bird weights vary across the region. The ecologist hypothesizes that birds closer to the coast weigh more because they have more choices of prey, whereas birds farther from the coast weigh less because they have less hunting options. The ecologist randomly selects 3 birds that live and hunt closer to the coast (within 10 miles) and 2 birds that live and hunt farther from the coast (10 to 20 miles away). The ecologist is unsure of what the rejection region should be for a Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a type I error rate of 0.20.
    1. Which of the following is the correct pair of null and alternative hypotheses for the ecologist's test? Let μ_1 be the population mean weight for birds closer to the coast and μ_2 be the population mean weight for birds farther from the coast.
    1. The ecologist labeled one sample \(X\) because it was the smaller sample, and one sample \(Y\) because it was the larger sample. The ecologist combined both samples into one sample of five observations, then ranked the observations from smallest to largest. How many different combinations of ranks can come from the observations in the \(X\) sample?

The sample labeled \(X\) is the sample with weights from birds that live farther from the coast. This means that this sample has 2 observations.

There are 5 total observations in the pooled sample, which means that there are 5 total possible ranks (1, 2, 3, 4, 5). Two ranks will belong to the \(X\) sample. Therefore, there are \(\binom{5}{2}=10\) possible combinations of ranks for the two observations in the \(X\) sample.

    1. The test statistic, \(w\), is the sum of the ranks of observations in the combined sample that belong to the smallest sample, \(X\). Calculate the probability that each of the following values of \(w\) will be realized assuming that \(H_0\) is true.
    • \(P(w=3)=\)
    • \(P(w=4)=\)
    • \(P(w=5)=\)
    • \(P(w=6)=\)
    • \(P(w=7)=\)
    • \(P(w=8)=\)
    • \(P(w=9)=\)

To find the probability for each value of \(w\), you must first list out all of the possible combinations of the ranks that the two observations from \(X\) can take on. For each combination of ranks, calculate the test statistic value.

\(\\\)

\(\text{Combination 1: (1, 2); w=3}\\\) \(\text{Combination 2: (1, 3); w=4}\\\) \(\text{Combination 3: (1, 4); w=5}\\\) \(\text{Combination 4: (2, 3); w=5}\\\) \(\text{Combination 5: (1, 5); w=6}\\\) \(\text{Combination 6: (2, 4); w=6}\\\) \(\text{Combination 7: (2, 5); w=7}\\\) \(\text{Combination 8: (3, 4); w=7}\\\) \(\text{Combination 9: (3, 5); w=8}\\\) \(\text{Combination 10: (4, 5); w=9}\\\)

\(\\\)

Under the null hypothesis, each possible combination of ranks is equally likely.

\(\\\)

The probabilities under the null hypothesis are:

\(\\\)

\(P(w=3)=\frac{1}{10}=0.10\\\) \(P(w=4)=\frac{1}{10}=0.10\\\) \(P(w=5)=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{10}=0.20\\\) \(P(w=6)=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{10}=0.20\\\) \(P(w=7)=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{10}=0.20\\\) \(P(w=8)=\frac{1}{10}=0.10\\\) \(P(w=9)=\frac{1}{10}=0.10\\\)

    1. Report the rejection region necessary for the Wilcoxon rank-sum test to have a type I error rate of approximately 0.20.
    • Reject \(H_0\) whenever \(w \ge\)

The Type I error rate is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis given that the null hypothesis is true. Since the probability of getting a test statistic value, \(w\), of 8 or 9 is 0.2 (0.1+0.1) the rejection region includes 8 and 9. That is, \(R = \{w : w \ge 8\} = \{8, 9\}\)

\(\text{Computing the test statistic value, } k: \\\) \(k=\frac{12}{N(N+1)} \sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{R_i^2}{n_i}-3(N+1)\\\) \(k=\frac{12}{18(18+1)} (\frac{48^2}{6}+\frac{44^2}{6}+\frac{79^2}{6})-3(18+1)\\\) \(k=4.2924\\\) \(\text{Degrees of freedom: }k-1=3-1=2\\\) \(\text{p-value: pchisq(4.2924, 2, lower.tail=F)}=0.1169\)

  1. Odontoblasts are cells located on the outer layer of a tooth's pulp that produce dentin and aid in tooth growth. An oral health researcher is studying whether ascorbic acid, a form of vitamin C, has a dose dependent effect on tooth growth as measured by odontoblast length (longer odontoblasts mean more tooth growth). The researcher has access to the ToothGrowth dataset in R, which has the odontoblast lengths in guinea pigs who received different doses of ascorbic acid. Use this data to test the researcher's question.
    1. Access the ToothGrowth dataset in R using the data function. Then, subset the dataset to remove all guinea pigs that received orange juice instead of ascorbic acid. This will aid in performing data visualization and running tests. (Hint: in the ToothGrowth dataset, VC represents ascorbic acid and OJ represents orange juice)
#Load ToothGrowth data
data(ToothGrowth)

#Subset the ToothGrowth dataset to only include data 
#for Guinea Pigs that received ascorbic acid
ToothGrowth = ToothGrowth[ToothGrowth$supp=="VC",]
    1. Create a side-by-side box plot of the length of odontoblasts for each dose of ascorbic acid.
#Create a side by side box plot of the length of

#so we must use the as.factor() function 
#to transform the dose column into a factor

boxplot(len~as.factor(dose),
        data=ToothGrowth,
        main="Odontoblast Lengths by Dose",
        xlab = "Dose of Ascorbic Acid",
        ylab = "Length of Odontoblasts",
        col = c("lightblue",
                "darkblue",
                "green"))

#median odontoblast length is the same for all 
#three doses of ascorbic acid.

             data=ToothGrowth)

  1. The Snowy owl is an endangered bird that lives in the northern regions of the North Pole. A zoo in southeast Texas is housing ten Snowy owls--four males and six females--as part of their owl conservation effort. The head zookeeper is unsure of what soil is best suited for nest building, and whether the owl's gender affects their preferred soil type. The zookeeper created five half-built nests on cold, hard soil and five half-built nests on cold, soft soil in the owls' enclosure. The zookeeper then released the ten birds into their enclosure and recorded which type of soil each owl chose to finish their nest. The zookeeper knows that each owl must choose one half-built nest for survival. The results are below.
##         
##          Hard Soil Soft Soil
##   Female         4         2
##   Male           1         3

    1. Select the appropriate pair of null and alternative hypotheses for this test.
    1. Calculate the probability of each of the following events occurring. This is the first step in calculating the p-value. Round your answers to four decimal places.
    • What is the probability that, of the female owls, 4 will select the hard soil and 2 will select the soft soil to build their nest?
    • What is the probability that, of the female owls, 5 will select the hard soil and 1 will select the soft soil to build their nest (this scenario is more "extreme" than the previous scenario)?
    • What is the probability that, of the male owls, 3 will select the hard soil and 1 will select the soft soil to build their nest (since this is a two-tailed test, we must check for extreme events in the opposite direction. That is, the direction in which most males select hard soil to build their nest).
    • What is the probability that, of the male owls, 4 will select the hard soil and 0 will select the soft soil to build their nest (this scenario is more "extreme" than the previous scenario).

Each of these events represents a certain configuration of the contingency table. Since the row and column totals in the contingency table were fixed by the zookeeper at the start of the experiment, a change in the value of one cell will change the values in all other cells. Start with the probability of the result of the experiment: that 4 females select hard soil and 2 select soft soil. This means that 1 male must select hard soil and 3 must select soft soil. Use the hypergeometric distribution to solve for the probability. This probability is: \(P=\frac{\binom{5}{4}\binom{5}{2}}{\binom{10}{6}}=0.2381\\\) \(\\\) When calculating the p-value, you need to calculate the probability of events occurring that are as or more extreme than the observed event. A more extreme event would be if 5 females selected hard soil and 1 selected soft soil. Then, 0 males would select hard soil and 4 would select soft soil. This probability is: \(P=\frac{\binom{5}{5}\binom{5}{1}}{\binom{10}{6}}=0.0238\\\) \(\\\) Since this is a two-tailed test, we need to calculate the probability of extreme events occurring in the other direction. In this case, the "other direction" references events in which most male owls choose to build their nest on hard soil. The first event would be if 3 male owls selected the hard soil and 1 selected the soft soil. Then, 2 female owls would have to select the hard soil and 4 would select the soft soil. This probability is: \(P=\frac{\binom{5}{3}\binom{5}{1}}{\binom{10}{4}}=0.2381\\\) \(\\\) An even more extreme event in this direction would be if 4 male owls selected the hard soil and 0 selected the soft soil. Then, 1 female owl would have to select the hard soil and 5 would have to select the soft soil. This probability is: \(P=\frac{\binom{5}{4}\binom{5}{0}}{\binom{10}{4}}=0.0238\\\)

    1. Report p-value for the test (to calculate the p-value, sum the probability values for the events in part b.). Round your answer to four decimal places.
    • p-value:

\(\text{p-value}=0.2381+0.0238+0.2381+ 0.0238=0.5238\\\)

    1. Assume that the zookeeper wants a type I error rate of 0.10. Which of the following conclusions can the zookeeper make?
  1. An infectious disease doctor at a prominent research university hypothesizes that the probability of a person catching the flu is related to whether that person uses mouthwash regularly. To test this hypothesis, the doctor randomly selected 16 people to participate in a study. Within the study, the doctor randomly selected 10 people and asked them to use mouthwash regularly (twice per day) for one month. The other 6 people were asked to not use mouthwash. After one month, all 16 people were exposed to a flu-like pathogen in a controlled environment. The doctor knows that a total of 7 people got symptoms, and 9 people did not get symptoms. The doctor created a contingency table, shown below, to match the mouthwash groups with the symptom groups.
##              
##               No Mouthwash Used Mouthwash
##   No Symptoms            1              8
##   Symptoms               5              2

    1. Select the appropriate pair of null and alternative hypotheses for this test.
    1. Calculate the probability of the experimental result occurring under the null hypothesis. Then, calculate the probability of more extreme events occurring in both directions under the null hypothesis (hint: Use the hypergeometric distribution). Round your answers to four decimal places.
    • What is the probability of the experimental result occurring under the null hypothesis? That is, what is the probability that, of those that regularly used mouthwash, 2 developed symptoms and 8 did not develop symptoms?
    • What is the probability that, of those that regularly used mouthwash, 1 developed symptoms and 9 did not develop symptoms (this scenario is more "extreme" than the previous scenario)? \(*10^{-4}\)
    • What is the probability that, of those that did not regularly use mouthwash, 0 developed symptoms and 6 did not develop symptoms (this scenario is as or more "extreme" than the previous scenarios, but in the opposite direction since this is a two-tailed test. The "other direction" refers to events in which more people in the mouthwash group get sick than in the no mouthwash group.).

Each of these events represents a certain configuration of the contingency table. The row and column totals were fixed by the doctor and by some of the experimental results (7 people developing symptoms and 9 not developing symptoms). When the row and column totals are fixed, a change in the value of one cell must change the values in all other cells so that the row and column totals do not change. Start with the probability of the result of the experiment: that of those that use mouthwash regularly, 2 get sick and 8 do not get sick. This means that of those not using mouthwash, 5 get sick and 1 does not get sick. Use the hypergeometric distribution to solve for the probability. This probability is: \(P=\frac{\binom{10}{2}\binom{6}{5}}{\binom{16}{7}}=0.0236\\\) \(\\\) A more extreme event would be if, in the mouthwash group, 1 person got sick and 9 people did not get sick. Then, 6 people in the no mouthwash group would get sick and 0 would not get sick. This probability is: \(P=\frac{\binom{10}{1}\binom{6}{6}}{\binom{16}{7}}=8.7413*10^{-4}\\\) \(\\\) Since this is a two-tailed test, we need to calculate the probability of extreme events occurring in the other direction. In this case, the "other direction" refers to events in which more people in the mouthwash group get sick than in the no mouthwash group. The only event in this direction that is as or more extreme than the previous two events would be if 0 members from the no mouthwash group got sick and 6 did not get sick. Then, 7 from the mouthwash group would get sick and 3 would not get sick. This probability is: \(P=\frac{\binom{10}{7}\binom{6}{0}}{\binom{16}{7}}=0.0105\\\) \(\\\)

    1. Report p-value for the test (to calculate the p-value, sum the probability values for the events in part b.). Round your answer to four decimal places.
    • p-value:

\(\text{p-value}=0.0236+8.7413*10^{-4}+0.0105=0.035\\\)

    1. Which of the following conclusions is correct assuming that the doctor wants to use a type I error rate of 0.05?
